title: What Bitcoin ETF flows reveal about institutional confidence - The Economic Times
content:
A critical distinction in interpreting ETF data was whether flows led price movements or followed them. An analysis of Bitcoin ETF flows since January 2024 found a stronger relationship between flows and Bitcoin’s preceding price performance than between flows and its subsequent performance. In other words, capital was generally more likely to enter after prices strengthened and leave after prices weakened. This pattern was consistent with investor behaviour across financial markets. Rising prices could reinforce confidence and encourage additional allocations, while falling prices could prompt investors to reduce their exposure. title: Do Bitcoin ETF Flows Really Predict Future Bitcoin Price Moves? This New Research Has Important Implications for BTC Investors.
content:
## Why Bitcoin ETF flows fall short

Every investor would like to have a (legal) edge of some kind. Still, a new study by DWF Labs confirms Bitcoin ETF flows aren't fortune-telling tools for a simple reason: Many investors make the quintessential mistake of performance chasing. In other words, they're reacting to what's already occurred, not what's upcoming.

The study notes that Bitcoin investors tend to exit spot ETFs following large declines and return to the funds after large rallies. That's called buying high and selling low when the better course of action is buying low and selling high. So, while the DWF Labs study notes some correlation between Bitcoin ETF flows and price, price moves first, and the flows/price relationship wanes within just a few days. [...] There are other reasons why Bitcoin ETF flows lack predictive power. Many crypto investors are HODLers, or devoted market participants, but the DWF study indicates those engaged with spot Bitcoin ETFs are jittery. Many sell these ETFs when Bitcoin slumps by just 7%. That's not even a correction, and it's nowhere near a bear market.

Arguably, the "weak stomachs" possessed by some ETF investors skew the potency of flows data because it's not unusual for Bitcoin to experience multiple declines of 7% (or more) over a few days or longer. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Thailand’s Supreme Court has ruled that Bitcoin qualifies as property under criminal law rejecting a defence argument that the cryptocurrency could not be stolen because it exists as electronic data and is not legal tender.

The court’s plenary bench said Bitcoin

 has a market price,
 can be exchanged for cash when a buyer is available, and

making it eligible for protection under property-related criminal laws.

“The value of the money transferred as property therefore fulfills the elements of an offense against property,” the court said in a translated summary. title: Crypto's Congress Problem is a Wiring Problem: Regulators Are Rewiring Anyway
content:
## Table of Contents

Following the US Senate's failure to pass the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act (CLARITY Act, H.R. 3633) on September 15, 2026, the SEC and CFTC stepped up to build an interim regime using existing administrative authority.

Although institutions can still access Bitcoin, the absence of a federal law means there are fewer long-term guarantees regarding regulatory permanence.

Resolving the year's most consequential cryptocurrency vote took only a few minutes on the floor, but the political stalemate followed over a year of intense bipartisan negotiations. [...] Access to a wider variety of digital assets can be significantly expanded by evolving custody frameworks.

Goldman Sachs' Q1 2026 portfolio reshuffle - where the bank fully unwound its XRP and Solana ETF exposures while maintaining roughly $700 million in core Bitcoin ETFs - serves as a cautionary tale regarding the highly tactical, liquidity-driven positioning of major institutional stakeholders.

Consequently, broad market breadth remains a supplemental allocation until market liquidity, index methodologies, and institutional-grade custody solutions fully mature.

Looking ahead, upcoming midterm elections warrant close observation, as the resulting legislative shifts will heavily impact the trajectory of the crypto regulatory environment. [...] What Actually Failed

Rather than structural problems, political considerations were at the heart of the setback. The primary concern with the measure, as stated by FinTech Weekly, was not the separation of authority between the SEC and the CFTC.

Instead, disagreement arose about the moral standards that govern the use of Bitcoin by government employees. A number of Democrats were most concerned about an ethics provision that would have barred presidents and other public officials from profiting financially from the sector while in office.

They felt the divestiture wording was so vague that the president could easily get around it, and they were worried about the Justice Department becoming an enforcer.

According to Republicans, both parties were in talks.
